back: One go at an experiment, e.g. one toss of a coin or one drop of a drawing pin.
$\dfrac{\text{number of times the outcome happened}}{\text{total number of trials}}$
Another name for relative frequency: an estimate of a probability from an experiment.

front: Expected number of times an outcome happens

back: As the number of trials increases, the relative frequency tends to get closer to the true probability.

front: Why do two sets of 20 trials give different results?
back: Chance variation: random results always vary, especially with few trials.
Using something random (dice, spinners, random numbers) to model a real situation and run many trials quickly.

front: Give an example of a probability you can only find by experiment
back: A drawing pin landing point up, or a bottle cap landing top up. The outcomes aren't equally likely.

front: How do you combine results from several groups?
back: Add all the successes and divide by all the trials (don't average the relative frequencies).

front: Reasons an experiment might not match the theory
back: Chance variation, too few trials, a biased object, or recording mistakes.
